The two groups diverge sharply after the ceasefire (@fig-event-study-intengroup). Pre-treatment coefficients for both are small and jointly insignificant (pre-trends Wald test p-value = `r round(pt_int$p_value, 3)`), so both series clear the parallel-trends bar. 

After the ceasefire, municipalities with high FARC exposure exhibit a pronounced and persistent decline in higher-education access, with point estimates reaching roughly 2 percentage points below those of unexposed municipalities in the medium run and remaining negative for several years. By contrast, municipalities with lower exposure experience smaller short-run declines and a faster recovery, with estimates gradually converging toward zero and becoming positive in later periods. However, the estimated effects for both groups are imprecise and statistically insignificant, limiting confidence in these differences.

Consistent with the descriptive evidence based on the continuous measure of conflict exposure, the results suggest that municipalities more heavily affected by violence experienced smaller and slower improvements in immediate access to higher education. This pattern may reflect persistent structural barriers that constrain their ability to translate reductions in violence into improved educational outcomes. Although the individual estimates are not statistically significant, the consistent differences in trends across exposure groups point to potentially meaningful variation in the post-ceasefire adjustment process. The following section assesses whether this adverse pattern among highly exposed municipalities remains robust to potential violations of the parallel trends assumption.

## Heterogeneity by student sex {#sec-het-sex}

The analysis so far pools male and female students. However, the channels through which conflict affects higher-education access, including displacement, income shocks, and the costs of attending institutions located far from home, may differ by gender. Moreover, a large literature suggests that female educational attainment is particularly sensitive to insecurity and mobility constraints. To explore this heterogeneity, I re-estimate the high-exposure specification separately for women and men, using municipality-year outcomes and pre-ceasefire exam-taker weights computed for each sex.

```{r het-sex}
#| include: false
sexcols <- grep("^pro_he_[A-Za-z]", names(df), value = TRUE)          # pro_he_F, pro_he_M
takcols <- sub("^pro_he_", "numstudents_", sexcols)

dsx <- df |>
  select(cod_mpio, all_of(dept), year, cease, intensity, did_presence,
         all_of(sexcols), all_of(takcols)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(all_of(sexcols), all_of(takcols)),
               names_to = c(".value", "sex"),
               names_pattern = "(pro_he|numstudents)_(.+)") |>
  mutate(female = as.integer(sex == "F"))
wsx <- dsx |> filter(year %in% 2010:2014) |> group_by(cod_mpio, sex) |>
  summarise(w_sex = mean(numstudents, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
dsx <- dsx |> left_join(wsx, by = c("cod_mpio", "sex")) |>
  filter(is.finite(w_sex) & w_sex > 0)
dsx_hu <- dsx |> filter(intensity %in% c("unexposed", "high")) |>
  mutate(treat_h = as.integer(intensity == "high"), did_h = cease * treat_h)

cfx <- function(m, term) {
  ct <- as.data.frame(coeftable(m)); nm <- rownames(ct)
  t  <- if (grepl(":", term)) nm[grepl("did_h", nm) & grepl("female", nm)][1] else term
  c(est = 100 * ct[t, "Estimate"], p = ct[t, "Pr(>|t|)"])
}
fes <- function(s) feols(as.formula(sprintf("pro_he ~ did_h | %s", fe)),
                         data = filter(dsx_hu, sex == s), weights = ~w_sex, cluster = ~cod_mpio)
mM <- fes("M"); mF <- fes("F")
mP <- feols(as.formula(sprintf("pro_he ~ did_h + did_h:female + female:cease | cod_mpio^sex + %s^year", dept)),
            data = dsx_hu, weights = ~w_sex, cluster = ~cod_mpio)
sxM <- cfx(mM, "did_h"); sxF <- cfx(mF, "did_h"); sxD <- cfx(mP, "did_h:female")

# extensive margin (any exposure) by sex
bpres <- function(s) cfx(feols(as.formula(sprintf("pro_he ~ did_presence | %s", fe)),
                          data = filter(dsx, sex == s), weights = ~w_sex, cluster = ~cod_mpio),
                         "did_presence")
sxMp <- bpres("M"); sxFp <- bpres("F")

esx <- function(s) feols(as.formula(sprintf("pro_he ~ i(year, treat_h, ref = %d) | %s", ref_year, fe)),
                         data = filter(dsx_hu, sex == s), weights = ~w_sex, cluster = ~cod_mpio)
mMe <- esx("M"); mFe <- esx("F")
prepat <- paste(min(df$year):(ref_year - 1), collapse = "|")
prem <- as.numeric(fixest::wald(mMe, paste0("year::(", prepat, "):treat_h"))["p"])
pref <- as.numeric(fixest::wald(mFe, paste0("year::(", prepat, "):treat_h"))["p"])
```

The estimates fall more on women (@tbl-het-sex). For male students the high-exposure ATT is `r sprintf("%.2f", sxM["est"])` percentage points and for female students it is `r sprintf("%.2f", sxF["est"])` percentage points, over half again as large. Pooling the two into a single interaction, the female–male difference is `r sprintf("%.2f", sxD["est"])` percentage points and is itself statistically significant, so the gap is not merely a matter of one estimate clearing a significance threshold and the other not. Both series clear their pre-trends test (Wald p-value = `r sprintf("%.2f", prem)` for men, `r sprintf("%.2f", pref)` for women), so the gap does not reflect differential pre-existing trajectories.

```{r tbl-het-sex}
#| tbl-cap: "ATT on higher-education access by student sex and treatment definition"
xrow <- function(m, term, label) {
  ct <- as.data.frame(coeftable(m)); nm <- rownames(ct)
  t  <- if (grepl(":", term)) nm[grepl("did_h", nm) & grepl("female", nm)][1] else term
  tibble(Specification = label,
         Estimate = 100 * ct[t, "Estimate"],
         SE       = 100 * ct[t, "Std. Error"],
         `p-value`= ct[t, "Pr(>|t|)"])
}
n_high_sex  <- function(s) dsx_hu |> filter(sex == s, intensity == "high", !is.na(pro_he), !is.na(w_sex)) |> distinct(cod_mpio) |> nrow()
n_high_both <- dsx_hu |> filter(intensity == "high") |> distinct(cod_mpio) |> nrow()
n_exp_sex   <- function(s) dsx |> filter(sex == s, intensity != "unexposed", !is.na(pro_he), !is.na(w_sex)) |> distinct(cod_mpio) |> nrow()
mMp <- feols(as.formula(sprintf("pro_he ~ did_presence | %s", fe)), data = filter(dsx, sex == "M"), weights = ~w_sex, cluster = ~cod_mpio)
mFp <- feols(as.formula(sprintf("pro_he ~ did_presence | %s", fe)), data = filter(dsx, sex == "F"), weights = ~w_sex, cluster = ~cod_mpio)

bind_rows(
  xrow(mMp, "did_presence", "Any exposure, male (pp)"),
  xrow(mFp, "did_presence", "Any exposure, female (pp)"),
  xrow(mM,  "did_h",        "High exposure, male (pp)"),
  xrow(mF,  "did_h",        "High exposure, female (pp)"),
  xrow(mP,  "did_h:female", "Female-male gap, high exp. (pp)")
) |>
  mutate(`Treated mun.` = c(n_exp_sex("M"), n_exp_sex("F"), n_high_sex("M"), n_high_sex("F"), n_high_both),
         `Obs`          = c(nobs(mMp), nobs(mFp), nobs(mM), nobs(mF), nobs(mP)),
         `R-squared`    = c(fixest::r2(mMp, "r2"), fixest::r2(mFp, "r2"), fixest::r2(mM, "r2"), fixest::r2(mF, "r2"), fixest::r2(mP, "r2"))) |>
  mutate(`p-value` = ifelse(`p-value` < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", `p-value`)),
         across(c(Estimate, SE), ~sprintf("%.2f", .x)),
         `Obs` = format(`Obs`, big.mark = ","),
         `R-squared` = sprintf("%.3f", `R-squared`)) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", rep("c", 6))) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", full_width = FALSE) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "5cm") |>
  footnote(general = paste(
    "Note: ATT on the immediate higher-education transition rate by student sex, under two treatment definitions, any FARC exposure (binary, first two rows) and high exposure only (high versus unexposed), each estimated separately for male and female students with municipality and department-by-year fixed effects, weighted by each municipality's 2010-2014 sex-specific average number of exam-takers, and standard errors clustered by municipality.",
    "The final row is the female-minus-male difference in the high-exposure effect, from a pooled specification that interacts the effect with a female indicator, with municipality-by-sex and department-by-year fixed effects.",
    "Treated mun. counts the treated municipalities identifying each estimate, 'Obs' the observations, and 'R-squared' the model fit."),
    general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE)
```

```{r fig-het-sex}
#| fig-cap: "Event study of the high-exposure effect on higher-education access, by student sex."
tdy <- function(m, var) {
  ct <- as.data.frame(coeftable(m)); ci <- as.data.frame(confint(m))
  ct$term <- rownames(ct); ct$lo <- ci[ct$term, 1]; ct$hi <- ci[ct$term, 2]
  ct <- ct[grepl(paste0("^year::.*:", var, "$"), ct$term), , drop = FALSE]
  ct$year <- as.integer(sub("^year::([0-9]{4}).*$", "\\1", ct$term))
  rbind(data.frame(year = ct$year, est = ct[["Estimate"]], lo = ct$lo, hi = ct$hi),
        data.frame(year = ref_year, est = 0, lo = 0, hi = 0))
}
bind_rows(transform(tdy(mMe, "treat_h"), sex = "Male"),
          transform(tdy(mFe, "treat_h"), sex = "Female")) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, est, colour = sex)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#c3c2b7") +
  add_ceasefire_line(ref_year) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.5), size = 2) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0.2, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, breaks = seq(-0.06, 0.06, 0.02)) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(min(df$year), max(df$year), by = 2),
    labels = seq(min(df$year), max(df$year), by = 2)
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.06, 0.06)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Male = farc_palette[["Unexposed"]], Female = farc_palette[["High"]])) +
  theme_capstone() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(size = rel(0.8))) +
  labs(colour = NULL, x = "Year", y = sprintf("Effect on immediate HE\ntransition rate (rel. to %d)", ref_year),
       title = "High-exposure effect by student sex",
       caption = paste(
         "Note: Outcome is the sex-specific municipal higher-education access rate (share of male or female Saber 11 exam-takers who",
         "\nenrol in higher education the following year). The event study compares high-exposure municipalities with unexposed municipalities,",
         "\nestimated separately by student sex. Estimates come from a weighted two-way fixed-effects specification with municipality",
         "\n and department-by-year fixed effects, weighted by each municipality's 2010-2014 average number of exam-takers of that sex,",
         "\nwith standard errors clustered by municipality. Points are coefficients relative to the 2013 reference cohort (the last cohort enrolling",
         "\nbefore the ceasefire) and bars are 95% confidence intervals. The dashed vertical line marks the 2013 reference year."))
```

The same asymmetry appears at the extensive margin. Pooling any FARC exposure, the ATT on men is indistinguishable from zero (`r sprintf("%.2f", sxMp["est"])` percentage points) while for women it is negative and marginally significant (`r sprintf("%.2f", sxFp["est"])` percentage points). These findings suggest that the binary specification in @sec-static-did masks substantial heterogeneity in treatment effects, particularly with respect to conflict intensity and a gendered penalty that appears to affect some groups more strongly than others.

# Robustness {#sec-robustness}

This section aims to evaluate if the negative high-exposure estimate depends on where the threshold between low and high exposure is drawn, on which municipalities serve as controls, or if it survives to modest violations of the parallel trend assumption (HonestDiD). 

To assess the robustness of the results to alternative treatment definitions and control group compositions, I conduct two robustness checks, each re-estimating @eq-static using the three-category specification. An additional robustness check, which reintroduces the country's main cities into the sample, is reported in @sec-appendix-cities. The benchmark being stress-tested throughout is the three-category high-versus-unexposed ATT of `r sprintf("%.2f", b_high)` percentage points from @sec-static-did.

## Sensitivity to violations of parallel trends (HonestDiD) {#sec-honestdid}

Since a passed pre-trends test is evidence of, rather than proof of, parallel trends [@RothSantAnnaBilinskiPoe2023], and @fig-event-study-intengroup displays a slight pre-ceasefire decline, I use the HonestDiD procedure of @RambachanRoth2023 to evaluate the robustness of the negative ATT for high-exposure municipalities. The method asks how large violations of parallel trends after the ceasefire would have to be, relative to the largest pre-treatment violation, to overturn the result.

```{r fig-honestdid}
#| fig-cap: "HonestDiD sensitivity of the high-vs-unexposed effect"
df_hu <- subset(df, intensity %in% c("unexposed", "high"))
df_hu$treat_high2 <- as.integer(df_hu$intensity == "high")
fml_hu <- as.formula(sprintf(
  "%s ~ i(year, treat_high2, ref = %d) | cod_mpio + %s^year",
  outcome, ref_year, dept))
m_hu <- feols(fml_hu, data = df_hu, weights = ~w_takers, cluster = ~cod_mpio)

es_vec <- function(model, pattern) {
  b <- coef(model); V <- vcov(model)
  idx <- grep(pattern, names(b))
  yrs <- as.integer(sub(".*year::([0-9]{4}).*", "\\1", names(b)[idx]))
  o <- order(yrs); idx <- idx[o]
  list(beta = b[idx], sigma = V[idx, idx, drop = FALSE], years = sort(yrs))
}
hu <- es_vec(m_hu, "year::[0-9]{4}:treat_high2")
numPre  <- sum(hu$years < ref_year)     # with 2010 in the panel: 3 (2010, 2011, 2012)
numPost <- sum(hu$years > ref_year)

# Report TWO targets so the parameter is not chosen for convenience:
#   - post-ceasefire average (consistent with a persistent decline)
#   - first post-period (2014)
run_rm <- function(l_vec) createSensitivityResults_relativeMagnitudes(
  betahat = hu$beta, sigma = hu$sigma,
  numPrePeriods = numPre, numPostPeriods = numPost,
  Mbarvec = seq(0, 2, by = 0.5), l_vec = l_vec)
# breakdown = largest Mbar whose robust CI still excludes 0
breakdown <- function(rm) { ex <- rm[rm$lb > 0 | rm$ub < 0, ]; if (nrow(ex)) max(ex$Mbar) else 0 }

l_avg    <- rep(1 / numPost, numPost)
l_first  <- basisVector(index = 1, size = numPost)
rm_avg   <- run_rm(l_avg)
rm_first <- run_rm(l_first)
bd_avg   <- breakdown(rm_avg)
bd_first <- breakdown(rm_first)

original_cs <- constructOriginalCS(
  betahat = hu$beta, sigma = hu$sigma,
  numPrePeriods = numPre, numPostPeriods = numPost, l_vec = l_avg)

# Same format as the appendix sex figure (@fig-appx-sex-honest): Original CI vs.
# robust CI across relative-magnitudes bounds, drawn as error bars.
hd_plot <- rbind(
  data.frame(x = "Original", lb = original_cs$lb, ub = original_cs$ub,
             method = "Original CI"),
  data.frame(x = as.character(rm_avg$Mbar[rm_avg$Mbar > 0]),
             lb = rm_avg$lb[rm_avg$Mbar > 0], ub = rm_avg$ub[rm_avg$Mbar > 0],
             method = "HonestDiD robust CI")
)
hd_plot$x <- factor(hd_plot$x, levels = c("Original", "0.5", "1", "1.5", "2"))

ggplot(hd_plot, aes(x = x, colour = method)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#121313") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lb, ymax = ub), width = 0.18, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(y = (lb + ub) / 2), size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Original CI" = farc_palette[["Unexposed"]],
                                 "HonestDiD robust CI" = farc_palette[["High"]])) +
  theme_capstone() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(x = expression(paste("Relative-magnitudes bound  ", bar(M))),
       y = "Effect on immediate HE transition rate \n(average post-ceasefire)",
       colour = NULL,
       title = "HonestDiD sensitivity — high vs. unexposed",
       caption = paste(
         "Note: Rambachan and Roth (2023) relative-magnitudes sensitivity analysis for the average post-ceasefire high-vs-unexposed",
         "\neffect on the higher-education access rate. The horizontal axis, Mbar, is the largest post-treatment violation of parallel trends",
         "\nallowed, expressed as a multiple of the largest violation observed in the pre-treatment period; Mbar = 0 imposes exact parallel",
         "\ntrends. 'Original CI' is the conventional 95% confidence interval; 'HonestDiD robust CI' is the robust confidence set."))
```
  

The sensitivity analysis qualifies rather than confirms the high-exposure result. For the average post-treatment effect and for the first post-treatment period, the robust confidence interval excludes zero only up to $\bar{M} =$ `r sprintf("%.1f", bd_avg)` and `r sprintf("%.1f", bd_first)`, respectively. Both fall below the natural benchmark $\bar{M} = 1$, which allows post-treatment deviations from parallel trends as large as the largest deviation observed in the pre-treatment period. Thus, although the estimated negative effect is statistically significant under conventional inference, it is not robust to even modest violations of the parallel-trends assumption. The result should therefore be interpreted as suggestive rather than definitive. It reflects a pattern in the data that holds under the identifying assumption, but whose credibility depends on the extent to which parallel trends can be deemed plausible in a setting with a small high-exposure group and potential geographic spillovers.

## A stricter threshold for heavy exposure {#sec-alt-threshold}

To assess the sensitivity of the results to the treatment classification, I redefine the low/high exposure threshold at the 75th percentile of the per-capita attack rate among exposed municipalities. Under this alternative specification, the high-exposure group consists of the top quartile of exposed municipalities rather than the top half.

```{r rob-threshold}
#| include: false

# Rebuild the three-category split at the 75th percentile among EXPOSED municipalities

pos_ex <- df |> 
  distinct(cod_mpio, attacks_pc) |> 
  filter(attacks_pc > 0) |> 
  pull(attacks_pc)
q75    <- quantile(pos_ex, 0.75, names = FALSE)

df_q <- df |>
  mutate(intensity75 = factor(case_when(attacks_pc == 0   ~ "unexposed",
                                        attacks_pc <= q75 ~ "low",
                                        TRUE              ~ "high"),
                              levels = c("unexposed","low","high")),
         did_low75  = cease * as.integer(intensity75 == "low"),
         did_high75 = cease * as.integer(intensity75 == "high"))

n_high75 <- df_q |> 
  filter(intensity75 == "high") |> 
  distinct(cod_mpio) |> 
  nrow()

# Fitting the model
m_arms_r <- feols(as.formula(sprintf("pro_he ~ did_low75 + did_high75 | %s", fe)),
                data = df_q, weights = ~w_takers, cluster = ~cod_mpio)

chk_thr <- grab(m_arms_r, "did_high75", "Top-quartile threshold")

# Clean high-vs-unexposed pre-trends under the stricter threshold
df_q_hu <- df_q |>
    filter(intensity75 %in% c("unexposed","high")) |>
    mutate(th75 = as.integer(intensity75 == "high"))

th75 <- "th75"
es_arms_r <- feols(as.formula(sprintf("%s ~ i(year, %s, ref = %d) | cod_mpio + %s^year", outcome, th75, ref_year, dept)), data = df_q_hu, weights = ~w_takers, cluster = ~cod_mpio)

pt_thr  <- wald_pre(es_arms_r, "th75")

att_thr <- chk_thr[["ATT (pp)"]]; p_thr <- chk_thr[["p-value"]]; ptp_thr <- pt_thr$p_value
```

Under the top-quartile threshold, high exposure is identified off `r n_high75` municipalities, and the high-versus-unexposed ATT is `r sprintf("%.2f", att_thr)` percentage points (@fig-robustness-forest), with pre-trends passed (joint Wald pre-trend test p-value = `r sprintf("%.3f", ptp_thr)`). The estimated effect is slightly larger than in the median-split benchmark and remains significant at the 5 percent level. This indicates that the finding is not driven by the choice of the cutoff. Restricting the high-exposure group to the most intensely affected quartile of municipalities strengthens, rather than attenuates, the estimated negative effect, even though the smaller group size leads to wider confidence intervals.

## A non-FARC comparison group {#sec-comparison-group}

A potential concern is that the estimated effect captures a broader post-conflict adjustment common to conflict-affected municipalities, rather than a mechanism specifically linked to the withdrawal of FARC activity. To address this concern, I restrict the comparison group to municipalities that experienced armed violence between 2010 and 2014 but were not exposed to FARC activity, using non-FARC-attributed events from the same six-category conflict measure. This approach excludes municipalities with no conflict exposure and redefines the identifying comparison as one between FARC-exposed municipalities and municipalities affected by other armed actors, following @PremVargasNamen2023.

```{r rob-compgroup}
#| include: false

nonfarc <- df |>
  filter(year %in% 2010:2014) |>
  group_by(cod_mpio) |>
  summarise(nofarc_tot = sum(total_nofarc_events, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(nofarc_exposed = as.integer(nofarc_tot > 0))

df_conflict <- df |>
  left_join(nonfarc, by = "cod_mpio") |>
  filter(treat_presence == 1 | nofarc_exposed == 1)

n_cg      <- length(unique(df_conflict$cod_mpio))
n_cg_ctrl <- length(unique(df_conflict$cod_mpio[df_conflict$treat_presence == 0]))

# Fitting the model
m_nofarc_r <- feols(as.formula(sprintf("pro_he ~ did_low + did_high_u | %s", fe)),
                data = df_conflict, weights = ~w_takers, cluster = ~cod_mpio)

chk_iii   <- grab(m_nofarc_r, "did_high_u", "Non-FARC comparison group")

# clean high-vs-unexposed pre-trends on the restricted sample
df_cg_hu  <- df_conflict |> 
  filter(intensity %in% c("unexposed","high")) |>
  mutate(thc = as.integer(intensity == "high"))

thc <- "thc"
es_nofarc_r <- feols(as.formula(sprintf("%s ~ i(year, %s, ref = %d) | cod_mpio + %s^year", outcome, thc, ref_year, dept)), data = df_cg_hu, weights = ~w_takers, cluster = ~cod_mpio)

pt_iii    <- wald_pre(es_nofarc_r, "thc")

att_iii <- chk_iii[["ATT (pp)"]]; p_iii <- chk_iii[["p-value"]]; ptp_iii <- pt_iii$p_value
```

With the comparison group narrowed to `r n_cg_ctrl` non-FARC-conflict-affected controls (`r n_cg` municipalities in total), the high-exposure ATT is `r sprintf("%.2f", att_iii)` percentage points (@fig-robustness-forest), with pre-trends again passed^[There is insufficient statistical evidence to reject the null hypothesis of parallel trends. The jointWald pre-trend test for the high-exposure category yields a p-value of `r sprintf("%.3f", ptp_iii)`]. The result is therefore unlikely to reflect differences between conflict-affected and conflict-free municipalities. Even relative to municipalities exposed to non-FARC violence over the same period, those with the highest levels of FARC exposure experienced larger declines in immediate access to higher education.

Taken together, the high-exposure estimate is negative in every specification. It remains statistically significant at the 5 percent level when heavy exposure is defined using a stricter top-quartile threshold, when the comparison group is restricted to municipalities affected by non-FARC violence, and when the country's largest cities are reintroduced into the sample (see @sec-appendix-cities). The estimated effect is therefore remarkably stable, both in sign and in magnitude, across the design and sample choices.

What the result does not withstand, however, is even a modest violation of the parallel trends assumption. As shown in @sec-honestdid, the estimated effect loses robustness once plausible violations from parallel trends are allowed. The remaining fragility is therefore tied specifically to the study's identifying assumption. For this reason, the dissertation characterises the high-exposure effect as suggestive and policy-relevant rather than conclusive.

```{r fig-robustness-forest}
#| fig-cap: "Robustness Checks for the High-Exposure ATT"

base_presence <- grab(m_pres, "did_presence", "Any exposure (binary)")
base_low      <- grab(m_arms, "did_low",    "Baseline: low vs. unexposed")
base_high_u   <- grab(m_arms, "did_high_u", "High vs. unexposed")
base_att <- base_high_u[["ATT (pp)"]]
base_p   <- base_high_u[["p-value"]]

bind_rows(base_presence, base_high_u, chk_thr, chk_iii) |>
  mutate(ci_low  = `ATT (pp)` - 1.96 * `SE (pp)`,
         ci_high = `ATT (pp)` + 1.96 * `SE (pp)`,
         arm = case_when(grepl("binary", Specification)            ~ "Any (binary)",
                         grepl("low",  Specification, ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "Low",
                         TRUE                                       ~ "High"),
         arm  = factor(arm, levels = c("Any (binary)", "Low", "High")),
         plab = sprintf("p = %.3f", `p-value`),
         Specification = fct_rev(fct_inorder(Specification))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = `ATT (pp)`, y = Specification, colour = arm)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#898781", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = ci_low, xmax = ci_high), height = 0.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = plab), nudge_y = 0.30, size = 3, colour = "#52514e",
            show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Any (binary)" = farc_palette[["Unexposed"]],
                                 "Low"          = farc_palette[["Low"]],
                                 "High"         = farc_palette[["High"]])) +
  scale_y_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.5, 0.9))) +
  scale_x_continuous( limits = c(-4, 2), 
  breaks = seq(-4, 2, by = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Effect on immediate higher-education access (pp)", y = NULL, colour = NULL,
       caption = paste(
         "Note: Each row is the pooled ATT (percentage points of the immediate higher-education transition rate)",
         "\nfrom re-estimating the three-category high-versus-unexposed design under a different specification or",
         "\nrobustness check. Colour denotes the exposure category (any/binary or high). Estimates come from a",
         "\nweighted common-timing two-way fixed-effects DiD with municipality and department-by-year fixed effects,",
         "\nweighted by 2010-2014 average exam-takers, and standard errors clustered by municipality. Markers are",
         "\npoint estimates, horizontal bars are 95% confidence intervals, and labels report the p-value; the dashed",
         "\nvertical line marks a null effect of zero."))+
  theme_capstone()

```

# Mechanisms {#sec-mechanisms}

The high-exposure result shows a relative decline in immediate higher-education access precisely where reductions in violence would predict the largest gains. This section explores the mechanisms behind this finding. I first show that the negative effect is driven by a composition effect: the access rate declined, but the number of students entering higher education did not, particularly in the smallest and most heavily exposed municipalities. I then rule out a set of alternative explanations, a coca opportunity-cost channel, differences in municipal fiscal capacity and spending, and a security-vacuum channel, none of which explains the observed pattern. Taken together, the evidence points to a supply-side absorption constraint concentrated in the smallest, most heavily exposed municipalities, and felt most acutely by women, rather than to any of these alternatives.

```{r mech-setup}
#| include: false
zscore <- function(x) (x - mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)

# pre-ceasefire population, log + z-scored: the size moderator
pop_z_df <- df |> filter(year <= 2014) |> group_by(cod_mpio) |>
  summarise(pop_pre = mean(poblacion, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(pop_z = zscore(log(pop_pre))) |> select(cod_mpio, pop_z)

# composition outcomes: denominator (takers), absolute numerator (HE-entrants)
dfm <- df |> left_join(pop_z_df, by = "cod_mpio") |>
  mutate(log_takers = log1p(numstudents),
         n_he       = numstudents * pro_he,
         log1p_nhe  = log1p(n_he))
dfm_hu <- dfm |> filter(intensity %in% c("unexposed", "high")) |>
  mutate(did_h = cease * as.integer(intensity == "high"))

# robust coefficient extractor (handles interaction-term name ordering)
cf <- function(model, term, mult = 1) {
  ct <- as.data.frame(coeftable(model)); nm <- rownames(ct)
  t  <- if (grepl(":", term)) {
    parts <- strsplit(term, ":")[[1]]
    nm[vapply(nm, function(x) all(vapply(parts, grepl, logical(1), x, fixed = TRUE)), logical(1))][1]
  } else term
  c(est = unname(mult * ct[t, "Estimate"]), p = unname(ct[t, "Pr(>|t|)"]))
}

# joint pre-trends Wald on a three-category event study (optionally one arm)
pre_pat_m <- paste(min(df$year):(ref_year - 1), collapse = "|")
wald_arm  <- function(model, arm = NULL) {
  pat <- paste0("year::(", pre_pat_m, "):intensity", if (is.null(arm)) "" else paste0("::", arm))
  as.numeric(fixest::wald(model, pat)["p"])
}
fitm_es <- function(yvar, data = dfm, w = NULL) feols(
  as.formula(sprintf("%s ~ i(year, intensity, ref = %d, ref2 = 'unexposed') | %s", yvar, ref_year, fe)),
  data = data, weights = w, cluster = ~cod_mpio)
```

## The rate fell, but access did not {#sec-mechanism-composition}

Higher education access is measured as the share of exam takers who enrol in higher education. Because both the numerator and denominator can change independently, the decline in the access rate does not necessarily imply fewer students reaching higher education. Decomposing the high-exposure effect into the two components shows that the negative rate does not reflect fewer students reaching higher education.

```{r mech-composition}
#| include: false
# absolute HE-entrants (numerator), three-category static and its pre-trends
m_abs    <- feols(as.formula(sprintf("log1p_nhe ~ did_low + did_high_u | %s", fe)),
                  data = dfm, cluster = ~cod_mpio)
abs_hi   <- cf(m_abs, "did_high_u")
m_abs_es <- fitm_es("log1p_nhe")
abs_pre  <- wald_arm(m_abs_es, "high")

# denominator (takers): grew, but pre-trends fail (high arm) -> caveat
m_tak    <- feols(as.formula(sprintf("log_takers ~ did_low + did_high_u | %s", fe)),
                  data = dfm, cluster = ~cod_mpio)
tak_hi   <- cf(m_tak, "did_high_u", 100)          # ~% change
m_tak_es <- fitm_es("log_takers")
tak_pre  <- wald_arm(m_tak_es, "high")
```

In the most heavily exposed municipalities the absolute number of immediate higher-education entrants did not fall after the ceasefire, by contrast it rose, the ATT is positive and statistically significant at 10% (@tbl-mech-composition), and this outcome shows no differential pre-trend^[There is insufficient statistical evidence to reject the null hypothesis of parallel trends. The joint Wald pre-trend test for the high-exposure category yields a p-value of `r sprintf("%.3f", abs_pre)`. See also @fig-mech-absaccess for study-event results.]. What fell was the rate, because its denominator, the number of exam-takers, grew faster than its numerator (@tbl-mech-composition). The negative result for the access rate does not indicate a decline in immediate access to higher education. Rather, it reflects a compositional effect driven by growth in the underlying population of exam takers.

```{r tbl-mech-composition}
#| tbl-cap: "High-exposure ATT on the immediate higher eduaction transition rate and its components (high vs. unexposed)"
comp_tab <- bind_rows(
  grab(m_arms, "did_high_u", "Transition rate (pp)"),
  grab(m_abs,  "did_high_u", "Absolute HE entrants (%)"),
  grab(m_tak,  "did_high_u", "Exam-takers (%)")
) |>
  rename(ATT = `ATT (pp)`, SE = `SE (pp)`) |>
  mutate(
    `Treated mun.` = c(
      n_high,
      dfm |> filter(intensity == "high", !is.na(log1p_nhe)) |> distinct(cod_mpio) |> nrow(),
      dfm |> filter(intensity == "high", !is.na(log_takers)) |> distinct(cod_mpio) |> nrow()),
    `Obs` = c(nobs(m_arms), nobs(m_abs), nobs(m_tak)),
    `R-squared` = c(fixest::r2(m_arms, "r2"), fixest::r2(m_abs, "r2"), fixest::r2(m_tak, "r2"))
  )

comp_tab |>
  mutate(`p-value` = ifelse(`p-value` < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", `p-value`)),
         across(c(ATT, SE), ~sprintf("%.2f", .x)),
         `Obs` = format(`Obs`, big.mark = ","),
         `R-squared` = sprintf("%.3f", `R-squared`)) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", rep("c", 6))) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position") |>
  footnote(general = paste(
    "Note: Each row reports the high-versus-unexposed ATT for one component of the immediate higher-education transition rate, from the three-category static two-way fixed-effects DiD with municipality and department-by-year fixed effects and standard errors clustered by municipality.",
    "The transition rate is in percentage points and is weighted by each municipality's 2010-2014 average number of exam-takers; the numerator (absolute immediate higher-education entrants) and denominator (exam-takers) are counts in log(1 + var), so their ATT reads approximately as a percentage change, and are unweighted.",
    "'Treated mun.' counts the high-exposure municipalities identifying the ATT, 'Obs' the municipality-year observations, and 'R-squared' the model fit.",
    "The positive numerator shows that absolute access did not fall: the negative rate reflects a faster-growing denominator, not fewer students reaching higher education."),
    general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE)
```

I refrain from attributing this expansion in the pool of exam-takers to the ceasefire. Although the number of exam-takers increased in highly exposed municipalities (approximately `r sprintf("%.0f", tak_hi["est"])`% relative to unexposed), which would be consistent with the rise in secondary retention documented for this agreement at lower schooling levels [@PremVargasNamen2023; @MontanoBardalesPalacios2025]. However, the exam-taker series fails the pre-trends test^[There is enough statistical evidence to reject the null hypothesis of parallel trends. The jointWald pre-trend test for the high-exposure category yields a p-value of `r sprintf("%.3f", tak_pre)`. See also @fig-mech-takers  for study-event results.]  , indicating that highly exposed municipalities were already following differential enrolment trajectories prior to the ceasefire. This pre-existing divergence undermines a causal interpretation of the post-ceasefire expansion, preventing its clean attribution to the ceasefire. Accordingly, I interpret the growth in the denominator as a measurement issue affecting the access rate rather than as evidence of a causal retention mechanism. The substantive conclusion therefore rests on the numerator, for which identification is more credible.

Regarding the gender gap highlighted in @sec-het-sex, an important question is whether the larger estimated penalty for women reflects a genuine reduction in women's access to higher education or also, a compositional effect arising from the denominator of the transition rate. Section @sec-appendix-sex addresses this issue and suggests two important findings.

First, the decomposition of the transition rate into its numerator and denominator also indicates that the larger female penalty is driven predominantly by composition rather than a reduction in educational access. In absolute terms, female access to higher education did not decline. It increased by roughly the same amount as male access. However, the number of female exam takers grew more rapidly, causing the female transition rate to rise less, or even fall, despite stable or improving enrolment counts. The estimated gender gap therefore reflects, to a large extent, a denominator effect rather than a deterioration in women's educational opportunities. The analysis also uncovers a more substantive pattern. In the smallest municipalities, the female disadvantage persists even when access is measured in absolute terms. This is precisely the setting in which @sec-mechanism-size identifies binding supply-side constraints.

However, the sex-specific level effects should be interpreted with caution. HonestDiD sensitivity analyses show that the estimates for women and men separately become fragile under even modest deviations from the parallel-trends assumption, much like the pooled effect (@sec-honestdid). The more defensible result is therefore not the magnitude of each sex-specific effect in isolation, but the gap between them. Because this gap compares women and men within the same municipality and year, many of the municipality-level trend violations that threaten the headline estimates are differenced out, making the heterogeneity result more credible than either level effect on its own.


## The shortfall concentrates in the smallest municipalities {#sec-mechanism-size}

If absolute access did not decline on average, an important question is whether the reduction in access rates documented in @sec-het-intensity was broadly shared across exposed municipalities or concentrated in particular contexts. To assess this, I examine heterogeneity by municipality size following the specification in @eq-ddd. The results indicate that the negative effect is concentrated among the smallest exposed municipalities.

```{r mech-size}
#| include: false
# rate penalty is size-dependent (continuous population moderation)
m_rate_pop <- feols(as.formula(sprintf(
  "pro_he ~ did_h + did_h:pop_z + pop_z:cease | %s", fe)),
  data = dfm_hu, weights = ~w_takers, cluster = ~cod_mpio)
rate_mean  <- cf(m_rate_pop, "did_h", 100)          # effect at mean-pop municipality (pp)
rate_sd    <- cf(m_rate_pop, "did_h:pop_z", 100)     # change per +1 SD log-pop (pp)

# denominator grows evenly by size; numerator grows MORE in large munis
m_tak_pop  <- feols(as.formula(sprintf(
  "log_takers ~ did_h + did_h:pop_z + pop_z:cease | %s", fe)),
  data = dfm_hu, cluster = ~cod_mpio)
tak_sd     <- cf(m_tak_pop, "did_h:pop_z", 100)     # % change per +1 SD log-pop (matches @tbl-mech-size)
m_nhe_pop  <- feols(as.formula(sprintf(
  "log1p_nhe ~ did_h + did_h:pop_z + pop_z:cease | %s", fe)),
  data = dfm_hu, cluster = ~cod_mpio)
nhe_sd     <- cf(m_nhe_pop, "did_h:pop_z", 100)     # % change per +1 SD log-pop (matches @tbl-mech-size)
```
 
@tbl-mech-size presents the results. Its first two rows describe the rate itself, in a municipality of average size the high-exposure effect on the rate is `r sprintf("%.2f", rate_mean["est"])` percentage points, and each additional standard deviation of population makes it `r sprintf("%.2f", rate_sd["est"])` percentage points less negative. The penalty is therefore deepest in the smallest municipalities and fades in the largest.

The final two rows help identify the source of this heterogeneity by estimating analogous population-size interactions for the numerator and denominator of the access rate. The number of exam-takers expands at essentially the same pace regardless of size, its size effect is `r sprintf("%.2f", tak_sd["est"])`% per standard deviation and is not statistically significant. The absolute number of students reaching higher education, by contrast, is what carries the size effect. It grows `r sprintf("%.2f", nhe_sd["est"])`% more per standard deviation of population^[Joint Wald pre-trend test for the high-exposure category, p-value = `r sprintf("%.3f", abs_pre)`]. Hence, after the ceasefire the pool of exam-takers grows by a similar proportion everywhere, but the number actually reaching higher education grows faster in large municipalities than in small ones, so the transition rate falls most where municipalities are smallest.

```{r tbl-mech-size}
#| tbl-cap: "Population-size moderation of the high-exposure effect on the immediate higher-education transition rate and its components (high vs. unexposed)"
n_high_rate <- dfm_hu |> filter(intensity == "high", !is.na(pro_he), !is.na(w_takers)) |> distinct(cod_mpio) |> nrow()
n_high_nhe  <- dfm_hu |> filter(intensity == "high", !is.na(log1p_nhe)) |> distinct(cod_mpio) |> nrow()
n_high_tak  <- dfm_hu |> filter(intensity == "high", !is.na(log_takers)) |> distinct(cod_mpio) |> nrow()

size_tab <- bind_rows(
  grab(m_rate_pop, "did_h",       "Rate: level at mean size (pp)"),
  grab(m_rate_pop, "did_h:pop_z", "Rate: change per +1 SD of size (pp)"),
  grab(m_nhe_pop,  "did_h:pop_z", "HE entrants: change per +1 SD of size (%)"),
  grab(m_tak_pop,  "did_h:pop_z", "Exam-takers: change per +1 SD of size (%)")
) |>
  rename(Estimate = `ATT (pp)`, SE = `SE (pp)`) |>
  mutate(
    `Treated mun.` = c(n_high_rate, n_high_rate, n_high_nhe, n_high_tak),
    `Obs`          = c(nobs(m_rate_pop), nobs(m_rate_pop), nobs(m_nhe_pop), nobs(m_tak_pop)),
    `R-squared`    = c(fixest::r2(m_rate_pop, "r2"), fixest::r2(m_rate_pop, "r2"),
                       fixest::r2(m_nhe_pop, "r2"), fixest::r2(m_tak_pop, "r2"))
  )

size_tab |>
  mutate(`p-value` = ifelse(`p-value` < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", `p-value`)),
         across(c(Estimate, SE), ~sprintf("%.2f", .x)),
         `Obs` = format(`Obs`, big.mark = ","),
         `R-squared` = sprintf("%.3f", `R-squared`)) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", rep("c", 6))) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", full_width = FALSE) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "4cm") |>
  footnote(general = paste(
    "Note: Each estimate comes from a triple-difference specification on the high-versus-unexposed sample that lets pre-ceasefire municipality population (log, z-standardised) moderate the high-exposure effect, with municipality and department-by-year fixed effects and standard errors clustered by municipality. The size slope is the change per one standard deviation of log population.",
    "The transition rate is in percentage points and weighted by each municipality's 2010-2014 average number of exam-takers. The numerator (absolute immediate higher-education entrants) and denominator (exam-takers) are counts in log(1 + var), so their estimates read approximately as percentage changes, and are unweighted.",
    "Treated mun. counts the high-exposure municipalities identifying each estimate, 'Obs' the municipality-year observations, and 'R-squared' the model fit."),
    general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE)
```

## Coca cultivation {#sec-mechanism-coca}

An alternative explanation is that the coca economy raises the opportunity cost of schooling. If the returns to illicit labour are higher in coca-growing areas, transitions to higher education may fall independently of the ceasefire [@Angulo2024; @RodriguezSanchez2012]. However, the results do not support this interpretation. The high-exposure effect does not vary with pre-ceasefire coca cultivation, and the relative reduction in access is statistically indistinguishable between coca-growing and non-coca-growing municipalities.

```{r mech-coca}
#| include: false
coca_base <- dfm |> filter(year <= 2014) |> group_by(cod_mpio) |>
  summarise(coca_pre = mean(coca_crops, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(high_coca = as.integer(coca_pre > 0))       # presence: coca is mostly zero
dfm_hu_c  <- dfm_hu |> left_join(coca_base, by = "cod_mpio")
m_coca    <- feols(as.formula(sprintf(
  "pro_he ~ did_h + did_h:high_coca + high_coca:cease | %s", fe)),
  data = dfm_hu_c, weights = ~w_takers, cluster = ~cod_mpio)
coca_mod  <- cf(m_coca, "did_h:high_coca", 100)
```

The interaction between the high-exposure effect and baseline coca cultivation is `r sprintf("%.2f", coca_mod["est"])` percentage points, statistically indistinguishable from zero (@tbl-mech-alt). This implies that the effect does not vary systematically with pre-ceasefire coca intensity and the decline in access is no greater in municipalities with higher levels of coca cultivation.

## Fiscal capacity and public spending {#sec-mechanism-moderators}

A related concern is that the estimated effect for highly exposed municipalities may reflect differences in local state capacity rather than exposure to FARC violence itself. To assess this possibility, I examine three measures of municipal fiscal capacity constructed from pre-ceasefire (2010-2014) per capita averages: fiscal revenue, total expenditure, and national government transfers. Each measure is dichotomised at its median and incorporated into a triple-difference specification by interacting it with the high-exposure treatment effect, following Equation @eq-ddd. A statistically significant interaction would indicate that the estimated effect varies with the municipality's fiscal capacity. As shown in @tbl-mech-moderators, none of the interaction terms is statistically significant. The negative effect observed in highly exposed municipalities therefore cannot be attributed to differences in municipal fiscal capacity or public spending, and appears to be broadly homogeneous across these dimensions.

```{r tbl-mech-moderators}
#| tbl-cap: "Public-finance moderators of the high-exposure effect (static triple interaction, high vs. unexposed)"
finmod <- df |> filter(year <= 2014) |> group_by(cod_mpio) |>
  summarise(pop = mean(poblacion, na.rm = TRUE), tax = mean(total_income_real, na.rm = TRUE),
            spend = mean(total_expenses_real, na.rm = TRUE),
            transf = mean(total_transfers_real, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(tax_pc = tax / pop, spend_pc = spend / pop, transf_pc = transf / pop,
         high_tax       = as.integer(tax_pc    > median(tax_pc,    na.rm = TRUE)),
         high_spend     = as.integer(spend_pc  > median(spend_pc,  na.rm = TRUE)),
         high_transfers = as.integer(transf_pc > median(transf_pc, na.rm = TRUE)))
dfa <- dfm_hu |> left_join(
  finmod |> select(cod_mpio, high_tax, high_spend, high_transfers), by = "cod_mpio")

modrow <- function(v, label) {
  m  <- feols(as.formula(sprintf("pro_he ~ did_h + did_h:%s + %s:cease | %s", v, v, fe)),
              data = dfa, weights = ~w_takers, cluster = ~cod_mpio)
  ct <- as.data.frame(coeftable(m)); term <- paste0("did_h:", v)
  n_high <- dfa |> filter(intensity == "high", !is.na(pro_he), !is.na(w_takers), !is.na(.data[[v]])) |>
    distinct(cod_mpio) |> nrow()
  tibble(Moderator      = label,
         Estimate       = 100 * ct[term, "Estimate"],
         SE             = 100 * ct[term, "Std. Error"],
         `p-value`      = ct[term, "Pr(>|t|)"],
         `Treated mun.` = n_high,
         `Obs`          = nobs(m),
         `R-squared`    = fixest::r2(m, "r2"))
}

bind_rows(
  modrow("high_tax",       "Fiscal revenue"),
  modrow("high_spend",     "Total expenditure"),
  modrow("high_transfers", "National transfers")
) |>
  mutate(`p-value` = ifelse(`p-value` < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", `p-value`)),
         across(c(Estimate, SE), ~sprintf("%.2f", .x)),
         `Obs` = format(`Obs`, big.mark = ","),
         `R-squared` = sprintf("%.3f", `R-squared`)) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", rep("c", 6))) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", full_width = FALSE) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "4cm") |>
  footnote(general = paste(
    "Note: Each row is a static triple-difference interaction between the high-exposure effect and one municipal public-finance moderator, estimated on the high-versus-unexposed sample with municipality and department-by-year fixed effects, weighted by each municipality's 2010-2014 average number of exam-takers, and standard errors clustered by municipality.",
    "Each moderator is a pre-ceasefire (2010-2014) per-capita average split at its median into a high indicator. The estimate is the interaction effect on the higher-education access rate in percentage points, and an estimate indistinguishable from zero means the high-exposure penalty does not vary with that characteristic.",
    "Treated mun. counts the high-exposure municipalities identifying each estimate, 'Obs' the municipality-year observations, and 'R-squared' the model fit."),
    general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE)
```

## A non-FARC security vacuum {#sec-mechanism-vacuum}

An important alternative explanation is that the ceasefire generated a security vacuum. To the extent that the FARC's withdrawal facilitated the expansion of other armed actors into its vacated territory [@Richani1997], any resulting increase in successor violence could depress educational transitions in highly exposed municipalities independently of the ceasefire's direct effects [@PenaDorussen2021]. I test this mechanism by examining post-ceasefire changes in non-FARC violence across all eleven SIEVCAC categories, rather than restricting attention to incidents involving the FARC.

```{r mech-vacuum}
#| include: false
vcats  <- c("WA","DP","AS","AT","DB","DF","MI","MA","RU","SE","VS")
vcols  <- paste0("n_eventos_", vcats, "_0")
vcols  <- vcols[vcols %in% names(dfm_hu)]
dfm_hu <- dfm_hu |> mutate(nofarc_all = rowSums(across(all_of(vcols)), na.rm = TRUE),
                           treat_hi   = as.integer(intensity == "high"))
m_vac    <- feols(as.formula(sprintf("nofarc_all ~ did_h | %s", fe)),
                  data = dfm_hu, cluster = ~cod_mpio)
vac_hi   <- cf(m_vac, "did_h")
# event study interacts year with the time-invariant treatment indicator
# (NOT did_h, which is zero in every pre-period year)
m_vac_es <- feols(as.formula(sprintf("nofarc_all ~ i(year, treat_hi, ref = %d) | %s", ref_year, fe)),
                  data = dfm_hu, cluster = ~cod_mpio)
vac_pre  <- as.numeric(fixest::wald(m_vac_es, paste0("year::(", pre_pat_m, "):treat_hi"))["p"])
```

According to the results in @tbl-mech-alt, there is no evidence of a surge in successor violence following the ceasefire. If anything, non-FARC violence declined more in highly exposed municipalities (`r sprintf("%.2f", vac_hi["est"])` events per municipality-year), the opposite of what a security-vacuum mechanism would predict. However, this specification fails the pre-trends test^[Joint Wald test for the high-exposure category, p-value = `r sprintf("%.3f", vac_pre)`] indicating that the two groups were already following different violence trajectories before the ceasefire. I therefore interpret these findings as providing no positive evidence of a violent vacuum, rather than as a definitive causal rejection of the hypothesis. 

```{r tbl-mech-alt}
#| tbl-cap: "Alternative-channel tests: coca cultivation and a non-FARC security vacuum (high vs. unexposed)"
mrow <- function(m, term, label, mult = 1) {
  ct <- as.data.frame(coeftable(m))
  tibble(Specification = label,
         Estimate = mult * ct[term, "Estimate"],
         SE       = mult * ct[term, "Std. Error"],
         `p-value`= ct[term, "Pr(>|t|)"])
}

n_high_coca <- dfm_hu_c |> filter(intensity == "high", !is.na(pro_he), !is.na(w_takers)) |> distinct(cod_mpio) |> nrow()
n_high_vac  <- dfm_hu   |> filter(intensity == "high", !is.na(nofarc_all)) |> distinct(cod_mpio) |> nrow()

alt_tab <- bind_rows(
  mrow(m_coca, "did_h:high_coca", "Coca cultivation interaction (pp)",        100),
  mrow(m_vac,  "did_h",           "Non-FARC violence DiD",     1)
) |>
  mutate(
    `Treated mun.` = c(n_high_coca, n_high_vac),
    `Obs`          = c(nobs(m_coca), nobs(m_vac)),
    `R-squared`    = c(fixest::r2(m_coca, "r2"), fixest::r2(m_vac, "r2"))
  )

alt_tab |>
  mutate(`p-value` = ifelse(`p-value` < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", `p-value`)),
         across(c(Estimate, SE), ~sprintf("%.2f", .x)),
         `Obs` = format(`Obs`, big.mark = ","),
         `R-squared` = sprintf("%.3f", `R-squared`)) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", rep("c", 6))) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", full_width = FALSE) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "4cm") |>
  footnote(general = paste(
    "Note: Tests of two alternative channels for the high-exposure penalty, both on the high-versus-unexposed sample with municipality and department-by-year fixed effects and standard errors clustered by municipality.",
    "Row 1 is the triple-difference interaction between the high-exposure effect and pre-ceasefire coca presence on the immediate higher-education transition rate (percentage points, weighted by each municipality's 2010-2014 average number of exam-takers); an estimate indistinguishable from zero means coca cultivation does not moderate the effect.",
    "Row 2 is the post-ceasefire high-versus-unexposed difference-in-differences on the count of non-FARC-attributed violent events per municipality-year (all eleven SIEVCAC categories, unweighted); a positive value would indicate a successor-violence vacuum, whereas the estimate is negative.",
    "Treated mun. counts the high-exposure municipalities identifying each estimate, 'Obs' the municipality-year observations, and 'R-squared' the model fit."),
    general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE)
```

# Limitations {#sec-limitations}

Several considerations are particularly relevant for interpreting the results. First, the measure of higher-education access captures only immediate transitions into higher education and therefore does not account for delayed enrolment. The estimates should consequently be interpreted as reflecting short-run access patterns. Second, because access is measured as a rate, changes in the outcome may arise from variation in either the numerator or the denominator. As shown in @sec-mechanism-composition, the negative high-exposure estimate is driven primarily by an expansion in the number of exam-takers rather than by a reduction in the number of students entering higher education. The results should therefore be interpreted with this compositional feature in mind.

Second, the armed-conflict data do not constitute a complete census of violent events. Underreporting may be more severe in municipalities with limited state presence, weak media coverage, or intense guerrilla activity, potentially introducing measurement error correlated with conflict exposure. Although the absence of an independent event-count dataset prevents a direct assessment of this bias, the fixed-effects design absorbs any time-invariant differences in reporting across municipalities. To the extent that underreporting is concentrated in areas of active conflict, it would more likely attenuate estimated effects than generate spurious ones. Nevertheless, this remains an important limitation and merits further investigation using alternative conflict and victimisation datasets.

Third, the peace process and the ceasefire were an agreement between the national government and the FARC guerrilla. Although this substantially reduced FARC-attributed violence, Colombia continues to experience violence from the ELN and from criminal organisations operating outside the formal armed conflict. The exposure measure used here captures only FARC-attributed violence reduction, so observed changes in immediate higher-education access could in principle be confounded by the continuation or intensification of violence from these other actors in the same municipalities. @sec-comparison-group addresses part of this concern directly, by showing the negative high-exposure result survives when the control group is restricted to municipalities that experienced non-FARC violence over the same period. However, it cannot rule out a subtler version of the concern, that ELN or criminal-group activity in FARC-exposed municipalities specifically changed after the ceasefire in ways correlated with, but not caused by, FARC's withdrawal, which @sec-mechanism-vacuum investigates as directly as the available violence registry allows.

Fourth, the identifying design relies on SUTVA, which requires that the potential outcomes of a municipality do not depend on the treatment status of neighbouring municipalities. This assumption may be difficult to sustain in the present context. FARC influence was geographically concentrated, and many low-exposure or ostensibly untreated municipalities bordered highly exposed areas. As a result, the ceasefire's effects may have spilled across municipal boundaries through several channels, including increased access to regional higher-education centres, broader economic and demographic recovery, and the reorganisation of armed actors across adjacent territories. To the extent that such spillovers occurred, they would most likely have benefited municipalities in the comparison group, attenuating the estimated treatment effect. Under this interpretation, the estimates reported in @sec-empirical-strategy and @sec-results should be viewed as conservative. Distinguishing direct effects from spillover effects is beyond the scope of the present dissertation and remains an important avenue for future research.

Finally, as in any difference-in-differences design, the results are only as credible as the parallel-trends assumption. @sec-event-study through @sec-honestdid report pre-trends tests and HonestDiD sensitivity analyses because a passed pre-test provides evidence for, but cannot validate, that assumption. The high-exposure level estimates, including the sex-specific results, appear sensitive to these assumptions (@sec-honestdid; @sec-appendix-sex). 

# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

This dissertation provides, to my knowledge, the first evidence on whether Colombia's post-conflict violence reduction extended beyond primary and secondary schooling to affect immediate access to higher education. The headline result, pooling any FARC exposure into a single binary treatment, is a null effect (@sec-static-did). But that null does not survive disaggregation by exposure intensity. @sec-het-intensity shows that in the municipalities that were most heavily exposed to FARC violence before the ceasefire, the immediate higher-education transition rate fell, relative to unexposed municipalities. This negative estimate is statistically significant and survives the robustness checks in @sec-robustness, but a HonestDiD sensitivity analysis shows it does not withstand more than a modest violation of parallel trends (@sec-honestdid). It is therefore suggestive rather than robust.

This pattern runs counter to the peace dividend mechanism motivating the dissertation. If improved security were driving the results (@sec-intro), higher exposure should be associated with greater gains in access, not relative losses. Section @sec-mechanisms tests several alternative explanations. The effect is not driven by a generic conflict-area effect, as it remains when the comparison group is restricted to non-FARC conflict municipalities (@sec-comparison-group). Nor is it explained by the coca economy (@sec-mechanism-coca). Finally, there is no evidence consistent with a violent security vacuum (@sec-mechanism-vacuum), although this test rests on weaker pre-trends evidence and cannot capture non-violent changes in local order.

What the mechanism analysis establishes is that the negative rate effect does not represent a decline in absolute access. As shown in @sec-mechanism-composition, the number of students entering higher education did not fall in heavily exposed municipalities. The rate declined because the pool of exam-takers expanded more rapidly than the number transitioning. A genuine reduction in absolute access appears only in the smallest and most heavily exposed municipalities (@sec-mechanism-size), and disproportionately among young women (@sec-het-sex). 

The most plausible reading of this localised shortfall is a supply-side constraint on access rather than a fall in demand. Higher-education provision in Colombia is concentrated in the larger cities and departmental capitals, and closing that rural access gap is itself an explicit aim of the peace agreement's rural-education agenda [@MEN2018a]. In the smallest and most remote municipalities, then, the post-ceasefire rise in secondary graduates outpaced the local capacity to absorb them: more students finished school and sat the exam, but the institutions, programmes, and places needed to enrol them did not expand at the same rate or within reach. This capacity gap is compounded by demand-side barriers that bind hardest in exactly these places, the direct and opportunity costs of enrolling [@LondonoVelezRodriguezSanchez2020], and the expense and disruption of moving to a distant city to study and it falls hardest on young women. The shortfall is therefore best understood as a deficit in the local supply and reach of higher-education opportunities, not as a decline in young people's aspiration to pursue them.

The results imply that policies designed to improve higher-education access may benefit from a more differentiated territorial strategy. Rather than relying exclusively on nationwide programmes, policymakers could prioritise municipalities with the greatest exposure to the conflict, where access constraints appear most persistent. Such a strategy is consistent with the mechanism analysis, which suggests that the main challenge lies not in educational demand but in the capacity of the higher-education system to absorb new graduates. If the spillover channels discussed in @sec-limitations are also present, the gains from targeted interventions may extend beyond the municipalities directly affected, further strengthening the case for place-based policy responses.

Equally important, these results suggest that reductions in violence do not automatically translate into greater educational opportunities. Nearly a decade after the signing of the the Peace Agreement, its implementation has remained uneven and incomplete, largely reflecting the political priorities and differing visions of successive governments [@Llorente2026]. While notable progress has been achieved in restorative justice and truth-telling processes, far less has been accomplished in tackling the structural territorial inequalities that the Agreement sought to address. Limited advances in education, healthcare, poverty alleviation, and rural development have constrained improvements in life opportunities across many former conflict-affected areas. In this context, the findings support the view that the institutional and socioeconomic conditions required to expand access to higher education remain insufficient, particularly in the municipalities most affected by the conflict.

# Appendix {#sec-appendix .unnumbered}

# Distribution of conflict events {#sec-appendix-events}

@tbl-events reports, for each of the eleven violence categories recorded by SIEVCAC during the pre-ceasefire period (2010-2014), the total number of events and their attribution across armed actors. For each category, the table shows the share attributed to the FARC, the share with no identified perpetrator, and the share attributed to other actors. The latter combines all non-FARC incidents, including both events attributed to other armed groups and those with unidentified perpetrators. The categories most strongly associated with FARC activity, namely war actions, selective killings, terrorist attacks, kidnappings, antipersonnel mines, and property damage, form the exposure measure used in @sec-treatment.

```{r tbl-events}
#| tbl-cap: "Distribution of armed-conflict events by type and attribution, 2010–2014"
vp <- readRDS(file.path(data_violence, "violence_panel2010_2024.rds")) |>
  filter(year >= 2010, year <= 2014)
ev_cats <- c(WA = "War actions",        DP = "Damage to settlements",
             AS = "Selective murders",  AT = "Terrorist attacks",
             DB = "Damage to property", DF = "Forced disappearance",
             MI = "Antipersonnel mines",MA = "Massacres",
             RU = "Recruitment",        SE = "Kidnappings",
             VS = "Sexual violence")
ev_raw <- purrr::map_dfr(names(ev_cats), function(s) tibble(
  type   = unname(ev_cats[[s]]),
  farc   = sum(vp[[paste0("n_eventos_", s, "_1")]], na.rm = TRUE),
  nofarc = sum(vp[[paste0("n_eventos_", s, "_0")]], na.rm = TRUE),
  unid   = sum(vp[[paste0("n_events_unid_", s)]], na.rm = TRUE))) |>
  arrange(desc(farc + nofarc))
ev_raw <- bind_rows(ev_raw, tibble(type = "Total", farc = sum(ev_raw$farc),
                                   nofarc = sum(ev_raw$nofarc), unid = sum(ev_raw$unid)))
pf <- function(x, t) ifelse(t > 0, sprintf("%.1f", 100 * x / t), "—")
ev_tab <- ev_raw |>
  mutate(total = farc + nofarc, other = pmax(nofarc - unid, 0)) |>
  transmute(`Event type`     = type,
            `Total events`    = total,
            `% FARC`          = pf(farc, total),
            `% Unidentified`  = pf(unid, total),
            `% Other actors`  = pf(other, total))
kbl(ev_tab, booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", "r", "c", "c", "c"),
    format.args = list(big.mark = ",")) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position") |>
  row_spec(nrow(ev_tab), bold = TRUE) |>
  footnote(general = paste(
    "Note: Total number of armed-conflict events per SIEVCAC category over the pre-ceasefire window (2010-2014), with the share attributed to the FARC, to unidentified perpetrators, and to other (non-FARC) armed actors.",
    "'Other actors' equals the non-FARC total net of unidentified events. The Total row aggregates all eleven categories."),
    general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE)
```

# Re-including the country's largest cities {#sec-appendix-cities}

The main analysis excludes Colombia's 13 largest cities from the construction of the exposure measure, as their size and socioeconomic characteristics make them poor comparators for the small and medium-sized municipalities where the FARC was most active. Reintroducing them therefore primarily adds unexposed or low-exposure municipalities to the comparison group. If the estimated effect for highly exposed municipalities were driven by their exclusion, the results should change materially once these cities are included.

```{r rob-cities}
#| include: false
base_all <- readRDS(file.path(data_final, "final_panel_2010_2023.rds"))

main_cities <- c("11001","05001","76001","08001","13001","68001",
                 "17001","52001","66001","54001","73001","23001","50001")
                 
df_city  <- base_all |> filter(!is.na(poblacion))            # keep the 13 cities
exp_city <- build_exposure(df_city, 2010:2014) |> filter(is.finite(attacks_pc))
med_pos_c <- median(exp_city$attacks_pc[exp_city$attacks_pc > 0])

exp_city <- exp_city |>
  mutate(treat_presence = as.integer(attacks_pc > 0),
         intensity = factor(case_when(attacks_pc == 0 ~ "unexposed",
                                      attacks_pc <= med_pos_c ~ "low",
                                      TRUE ~ "high"),
                            levels = c("unexposed","low","high")),
         farc_logint = log1p(attacks_pc))

panel_city <- df_city |>
  inner_join(select(exp_city, cod_mpio, attacks_pc, treat_presence,
                    intensity, farc_logint), by = "cod_mpio") |>
  mutate(cease = as.integer(year >= 2014),
         did_presence = cease * treat_presence,
         did_low = cease * as.integer(intensity == "low"),
         did_high_u = cease * as.integer(intensity == "high"))
n_cities_added <- length(intersect(unique(panel_city$cod_mpio), main_cities))

m_allmun_r <- feols(as.formula(sprintf("pro_he ~ did_low + did_high_u | %s", fe)),
                data = panel_city, weights = ~w_takers, cluster = ~cod_mpio)

chk_cities <- grab(m_allmun_r, "did_high_u", "Appendix: +13 largest cities")

att_city <- chk_cities[["ATT (pp)"]]; p_city <- chk_cities[["p-value"]]
```

Including the `r n_cities_added` largest cities and rebuilding the exposure split on the enlarged sample leaves the high-exposure ATT at `r sprintf("%.2f", att_city)` percentage points with a p-value of `r ifelse(p_city < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p_city))`. The estimate is essentially unchanged, confirming that the result is a feature of the FARC-exposed municipalities themselves rather than of the decision to set the big cities aside.

```{r rob-cities-es}
#| include: false
m_int_city <- feols(as.formula(sprintf(
  "%s ~ i(year, intensity, ref = %d, ref2 = 'unexposed') | cod_mpio + %s^year",
  outcome, ref_year, dept)),
  data = panel_city, weights = ~w_takers, cluster = ~cod_mpio)
df_int_city <- tidy_es(m_int_city, ref_year, group_var = "intensity")
df_int_city$group <- factor(df_int_city$group, levels = c("low", "high"))
ptp_cities <- wald_pre(m_int_city, "intensity")$p_value
```

The dynamic pattern is likewise largely unchanged. Re-estimating the three-category event study on the expanded sample that includes the largest cities (@fig-cities-eventstudy) reproduces the results reported in @sec-het-intensity. Following the ceasefire, the high-exposure group experiences a relative decline compared with the unexposed group, whereas the low-exposure group continues to track the latter closely. The pre-trends are somewhat weaker than in the baseline specification. Although the pre-treatment coefficients are jointly insignificant at the 5% level, they fail to do so at the 10% level (Wald p-value = `r sprintf("%.3f", ptp_cities)`), suggesting some caution in interpreting the dynamic estimates.

```{r fig-cities-eventstudy}
#| fig-cap: "Event study — three-category exposure intensity (low and high, each vs. unexposed), with the 13 largest cities re-included"
plot_es(df_int_city, "Exposure intensity, 13 main cities re-included",
        ref_year, grouped = TRUE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(min(panel_city$year), max(panel_city$year), by = 2),
                     labels = seq(min(panel_city$year), max(panel_city$year), by = 2)) +
  labs(caption = paste(
    "Note: Robustness re-estimate of the three-category event study with the 13 largest cities (excluded from the baseline) added back to the",
    "\nsample. The outcome is the municipal higher-education access rate. Exposed municipalities are split at the median per-capita FARC",
    "\nattack rate (2010-2014) into low- (green) and high-exposure (red) groups, each compared with the common unexposed group.",
    "\nEstimates come from a weighted two-way fixed-effects event study with municipality and department-by-year fixed effects, weighted",
    "\nby each municipality's 2010-2014 average number of exam-takers, with standard errors clustered by municipality. Points are",
    "\ncoefficients relative to the 2013 reference cohort (dashed line) and bars are 95% confidence intervals."))
```

# Composition dynamics: entrants and exam-takers {#sec-appendix-composition}

This section presents the dynamic counterpart to the static decomposition in @sec-mechanism-composition. It estimates event studies separately for the two components of the transition rate: the numerator, the number of students entering higher education, and the denominator, the number of exam-takers, by FARC-exposure intensity. The results show no decline in the absolute number of higher-education entrants in highly exposed municipalities (@fig-mech-absaccess). By contrast, the number of exam-takers increases (@fig-mech-takers), although the corresponding specification fails the pre-trends test and is therefore interpreted descriptively.

```{r fig-mech-absaccess}
#| fig-cap: "Event study — higher-education entrants by FARC-exposure intensity"
df_abs <- tidy_es(m_abs_es, ref_year, group_var = "intensity")
df_abs$group <- factor(df_abs$group, levels = c("low", "high"))
plot_es(df_abs, "Absolute higher-education entrants by exposure intensity", ref_year,
        grouped = TRUE, pct = FALSE, y_lab = sprintf("Effect on log(1 + HE entrants), rel. to %d", ref_year)) +
  labs(caption = paste(
    "Note: The outcome is the number of higher-education entrants per municipality, transformed as log(1 + entrants). This transformation",
    "\nis used because a small numberof municipality-years have no entrants. The vertical axis is in log points. Exposed municipalities are",
    "\nsplit at the median per-capita FARC attack rate (2010-2014), into low-(green) and high-exposure (red) groups, each compared with",
    "\nthe common unexposed group. Estimates come from a two-way fixed-effects event study with municipality and department-by-year",
    "\nfixed effects and standard errors clustered by municipality. Points are coefficients relative to the 2013 reference cohort and bars are",
    "\n95% confidence intervals. The dashed vertical line marks the 2013 reference year."))
```

```{r fig-mech-takers}
#| fig-cap: "Event study — exam-takers by FARC-exposure intensity"
df_tak <- tidy_es(m_tak_es, ref_year, group_var = "intensity")
df_tak$group <- factor(df_tak$group, levels = c("low", "high"))
plot_es(df_tak, "Exam-takers by exposure intensity", ref_year,

    "Note: The outcome is the number of Saber 11 exam-takers per municipality, the denominator of the transition rate, transformed as",
    "\nlog(1 + takers). The vertical axis is in log points. Exposed municipalities are split at the median per-capita FARC attack rate (2010-",
    "\n2014) into low- (green) and high-exposure (red) groups, each compared with the common unexposed group. Estimates come",
    "\nfrom a two-way fixed-effects event study with municipality and department-by-year fixed effects and standard errors clustered by",
    "\nmunicipality.Points are coefficients relative to the 2013 reference cohort and bars are 95% confidence intervals. The dashed vertical",
```
