# Sex heterogeneity: decomposition and sensitivity {#sec-appendix-sex}

@sec-het-sex reports that the high-exposure penalty on the higher-education transition rate is significantly larger for female than for male students. This appendix aims to answer two questions: is the larger female penalty a genuine fall in women's access, or as for the pooled result in @sec-mechanism-composition, an artefact of the rate's denominator; and how robust is it to violations of parallel trends (HonestDiD)?

```{r appx-sex}
#| include: false
# sex-specific weights, outcomes, clean high-vs-unexposed sample, size moderator
wS <- df |> filter(year %in% 2010:2014) |> group_by(cod_mpio) |>
  summarise(w_F = mean(numstudents_F, na.rm = TRUE),
            w_M = mean(numstudents_M, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
pz <- df |> filter(year <= 2014) |> group_by(cod_mpio) |>
  summarise(pp = mean(poblacion, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(pop_z = (log(pp) - mean(log(pp), na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(log(pp), na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  select(cod_mpio, pop_z)
dS <- df |> left_join(wS, by = "cod_mpio") |> left_join(pz, by = "cod_mpio") |>
  mutate(log1p_nhe_F = log1p(numstudents_F * pro_he_F), ltak_F = log1p(numstudents_F),
         log1p_nhe_M = log1p(numstudents_M * pro_he_M), ltak_M = log1p(numstudents_M))
dShu <- dS |> filter(intensity %in% c("unexposed", "high")) |>
  mutate(treat_h = as.integer(intensity == "high"), did_h = cease * treat_h)

hi <- function(m, term = "did_high_u") {
  ct <- as.data.frame(coeftable(m)); nm <- rownames(ct)
  t <- if (grepl(":", term)) nm[grepl("did_h", nm) & grepl("pop_z", nm)][1] else term
  c(est = unname(ct[t, "Estimate"]), p = unname(ct[t, "Pr(>|t|)"]))
}
fdec <- function(y, wt) feols(as.formula(sprintf("%s ~ did_low + did_high_u | %s", y, fe)),
                              data = dS, weights = wt, cluster = ~cod_mpio)
dFden <- hi(fdec("ltak_F", NULL)); dFabs <- hi(fdec("log1p_nhe_F", NULL)); dFrate <- hi(fdec("pro_he_F", ~w_F))
dMden <- hi(fdec("ltak_M", NULL)); dMabs <- hi(fdec("log1p_nhe_M", NULL)); dMrate <- hi(fdec("pro_he_M", ~w_M))

# female absolute access, moderated by municipality size
mFpop <- feols(as.formula(sprintf("log1p_nhe_F ~ did_h + did_h:pop_z + pop_z:cease | %s", fe)),
               data = dShu, cluster = ~cod_mpio)
fpop <- hi(mFpop, "did_h:pop_z")

# HonestDiD (relative magnitudes) on the sex-specific rate event studies
es_vec <- function(model, pattern) {
  b <- coef(model); V <- vcov(model); idx <- grep(pattern, names(b))
  yrs <- as.integer(sub(".*year::([0-9]{4}).*", "\\1", names(b)[idx])); o <- order(yrs); idx <- idx[o]
  list(beta = b[idx], sigma = V[idx, idx, drop = FALSE], years = sort(yrs))
}
bdn <- function(rm) { ex <- rm[rm$lb > 0 | rm$ub < 0, ]; if (nrow(ex)) max(ex$Mbar) else 0 }
hd <- function(y, wt) {
  m  <- feols(as.formula(sprintf("%s ~ i(year, treat_h, ref = %d) | %s", y, ref_year, fe)),
              data = dShu, weights = wt, cluster = ~cod_mpio)
  hu <- es_vec(m, "year::[0-9]{4}:treat_h"); nP <- sum(hu$years < ref_year); nQ <- sum(hu$years > ref_year)
  rr <- function(l) createSensitivityResults_relativeMagnitudes(
    betahat = hu$beta, sigma = hu$sigma, numPrePeriods = nP, numPostPeriods = nQ,
    Mbarvec = seq(0, 2, by = 0.5), l_vec = l)
  c(avg = bdn(rr(rep(1 / nQ, nQ))), first = bdn(rr(basisVector(index = 1, size = nQ))))
}
bdF <- hd("pro_he_F", ~w_F); bdM <- hd("pro_he_M", ~w_M)

# joint Wald pre-trend tests for the sex-specific decomposition components
esS <- function(y, wt) feols(
  as.formula(sprintf("%s ~ i(year, treat_h, ref = %d) | %s", y, ref_year, fe)),
  data = dShu, weights = wt, cluster = ~cod_mpio)
pF_rate <- wald_pre(esS("pro_he_F",    ~w_F), "treat_h")$p_value
pF_abs  <- wald_pre(esS("log1p_nhe_F", NULL), "treat_h")$p_value
pF_den  <- wald_pre(esS("ltak_F",      NULL), "treat_h")$p_value
```

## Rate decomposition analysis

Applying the numerator–denominator decomposition of @sec-mechanism-composition to each sex shows the larger female penalty is not, on average, a fall in women's absolute access (@tbl-appx-sex-decomp). Absolute female higher-education entrants rose after the ceasefire `r sprintf("%+.1f", 100*dFabs["est"])`% relative to unexposed municipalities) and almost identical to the male figure (`r sprintf("%+.1f", 100*dMabs["est"])`%). What differs by sex is the denominator.  The female exam-taker pool grew more (`r sprintf("%+.1f", 100*dFden["est"])`% versus `r sprintf("%+.1f", 100*dMden["est"])`% for men), so the female transition rate falls more (`r sprintf("%.2f", 100*dFrate["est"])` percentage points versus `r sprintf("%.2f", 100*dMrate["est"])` percentage points) even though the count of women reaching higher education does not. As in @sec-mechanism-composition, this female denominator channel fails its pre-trends test (joint Wald p-value = `r sprintf("%.3f", pF_den)`) and is read descriptively, whereas the female absolute-access and rate outcomes both pass it (joint Wald p-value = `r sprintf("%.3f", pF_abs)` and `r sprintf("%.3f", pF_rate)`, respectively).

```{r tbl-appx-sex-decomp}
#| tbl-cap: "Decomposition of the high-exposure effect by sex (high vs. unexposed)"
srow <- function(y, wt, wcol, label) {
  m  <- fdec(y, wt)
  ct <- as.data.frame(coeftable(m))
  d  <- dS |> filter(intensity == "high", !is.na(.data[[y]]))
  if (!is.null(wcol)) d <- d |> filter(!is.na(.data[[wcol]]))
  tibble(Component      = label,
         Estimate       = 100 * ct["did_high_u", "Estimate"],
         SE             = 100 * ct["did_high_u", "Std. Error"],
         `p-value`      = ct["did_high_u", "Pr(>|t|)"],
         `Treated mun.` = d |> distinct(cod_mpio) |> nrow(),
         `Obs`          = nobs(m),
         `R-squared`    = fixest::r2(m, "r2"))
}

bind_rows(
  srow("ltak_F",      NULL,  NULL,  "Exam-takers female (%)"),
  srow("ltak_M",      NULL,  NULL,  "Exam-takers male (%)"),
  srow("log1p_nhe_F", NULL,  NULL,  "HE entrants female (%)"),
  srow("log1p_nhe_M", NULL,  NULL,  "HE entrants male (%)"),
  srow("pro_he_F",    ~w_F,  "w_F", "Transition rate female (pp)"),
  srow("pro_he_M",    ~w_M,  "w_M", "Transition rate male (pp)")
) |>
  mutate(`p-value` = ifelse(`p-value` < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", `p-value`)),
         across(c(Estimate, SE), ~sprintf("%.2f", .x)),
         `Obs` = format(`Obs`, big.mark = ","),
         `R-squared` = sprintf("%.3f", `R-squared`)) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", rep("c", 6))) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", full_width = FALSE) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "4.5cm") |>
  footnote(general = paste(
    "Note: Sex-specific decomposition of the effect of high versus unexposed exposure on immediate higher education transition rates, estimated separately for female and male students using the three-category sample, with municipality and department-by-year fixed effects and standard errors clustered at the municipality level.",
    "The transition rate is in percentage points and weighted by each municipality's 2010-2014 sex-specific average number of exam-takers; the numerator (higher-education entrants) and denominator (exam-takers) are counts in log(1 + var), read approximately as percentage changes, and unweighted.",
    "Treated mun. counts the high-exposure municipalities identifying each estimate, 'Obs' the municipality-year observations, and 'R-squared' the model fit."),
    general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE)
```

The one genuine shortfall in women's absolute access is spatial, and it points back to the paper's mechanism. Moderating female absolute access by municipality size, the effect at an average-sized municipality is small and not significant (`r sprintf("%+.1f", 100*fpop["est"])`%), but access grows significantly more in larger municipalities and lags in the smallest. Women in the smallest, most heavily exposed municipalities are thus the group for whom absolute higher-education access genuinely falls short, the same places @sec-mechanism-size identifies as supply-constrained, and the group least able to leave home to reach a distant institution.

## Sensitivity to parallel-trends violations

The sex-specific levels do not survive a HonestDiD relative-magnitudes stress test (@fig-appx-sex-honest). For the average post-ceasefire effect, the robust confidence interval covers zero at the smallest violation considered for both sexes (breakdown $\bar M = 0$). Only the first post-period female effect tolerates a violation up to half the worst pre-period deviation (breakdown $\bar M =$ `r sprintf("%.1f", bdF["first"])`) before admitting zero. The sex-specific levels are therefore as fragile as the pooled high-exposure result of @sec-honestdid, and should be read as suggestive. Consequently, the most credible result is not the magnitude of the level effect for either female or male students, but the difference between them estimated in @sec-het-sex. Because this comparison is made within municipalities, it removes municipality-specific trends that affect both groups and that the sensitivity analysis identifies as a potential source of bias in the level estimates.

```{r fig-appx-sex-honest}
#| fig-cap: "HonestDiD relative-magnitudes sensitivity of the sex-specific high-exposure effect (high vs. unexposed)"
#| fig-height: 7.5
# Robust CIs across relative-magnitudes bounds, for each sex, stacked vertically.
sens_sex <- function(y, wt, sexlab) {
  m  <- feols(as.formula(sprintf("%s ~ i(year, treat_h, ref = %d) | %s", y, ref_year, fe)),
              data = dShu, weights = wt, cluster = ~cod_mpio)
  hu <- es_vec(m, "year::[0-9]{4}:treat_h")
  nP <- sum(hu$years < ref_year); nQ <- sum(hu$years > ref_year)
  l_avg <- rep(1 / nQ, nQ)
  rmv <- createSensitivityResults_relativeMagnitudes(
    betahat = hu$beta, sigma = hu$sigma,
    numPrePeriods = nP, numPostPeriods = nQ,
    Mbarvec = seq(0.5, 2, by = 0.5), l_vec = l_avg)
  ocs <- constructOriginalCS(
    betahat = hu$beta, sigma = hu$sigma,
    numPrePeriods = nP, numPostPeriods = nQ, l_vec = l_avg)
  rbind(
    data.frame(x = "Original", lb = ocs$lb, ub = ocs$ub, method = "Original CI"),
    data.frame(x = as.character(rmv$Mbar), lb = rmv$lb, ub = rmv$ub,
               method = "HonestDiD robust CI")
  ) |> transform(sex = sexlab)
}

sx_sens <- rbind(sens_sex("pro_he_F", ~w_F, "Female students"),
                 sens_sex("pro_he_M", ~w_M, "Male students"))
sx_sens$x   <- factor(sx_sens$x, levels = c("Original", "0.5", "1", "1.5", "2"))
sx_sens$sex <- factor(sx_sens$sex, levels = c("Female students", "Male students"))

ggplot(sx_sens, aes(x = x, colour = method)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#121313") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lb, ymax = ub), width = 0.18, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(y = (lb + ub) / 2), size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~sex, ncol = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Original CI" = farc_palette[["Unexposed"]],
                                 "HonestDiD robust CI" = farc_palette[["High"]])) +
  theme_capstone() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(x = expression(paste("Relative-magnitudes bound  ", bar(M))),
       y = "Effect on immediate HE transition rate \n(average post-ceasefire)",
       colour = NULL,
       title = "HonestDiD sensitivity by student sex",
       caption = paste(
         "Note: Rambachan and Roth (2023) relative-magnitudes sensitivity analysis of the average post-ceasefire high-vs-unexposed",
         "\neffect on the sex-specific higher-education access rate, estimated separately for female (top) and male (bottom) students. The",
         "\nhorizontal axis is the largest post-treatment violation of parallel trends allowed, Mbar, as a multiple of the largest pre-treatment violation.",
         "\n'Original CI' is the conventional 95% interval and 'HonestDiD robust CI' is the robust confidence set."))
```

# Replication material

All data and analytical workflows necessary for reproducing the reported results are hosted in the public GitHub repository X. The accompanying README file details the repository organisation, describes the contents of each folder and script, and outlines the procedures required for replication.
